title: Given a Scenario, Implement and Maintain Identity and Access Management

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Identity and Access Management (IAM) controls who receives an identity, how that identity is verified, what the identity may access, and how long the access should remain.
Objective 4.6 asks you to manage identity through the account lifecycle and select the authentication, authorization, password, and privileged-access control that fits a scenario.
Use this lifecycle: identify, authenticate, authorize, review, and remove access when it is no longer required.

entries.title: IAM Decision Pattern
paragraphs: Ask four questions: Who is the user? How is the identity proven? What is the minimum access required? For how long should that access exist?
entries.recognitionCue: Authentication proves who you are; authorization determines what you may do.

sections.title: Account Lifecycle and Identity Proofing
paragraphs: Secure IAM begins before a user signs in. The organization must verify the person, create the right account, assign only required permissions, and remove access promptly when circumstances change.

entries.title: Provisioning/De-provisioning User Accounts
paragraphs: Provisioning creates an identity and grants the access needed for a new user or role. De-provisioning disables or removes access when a person leaves, changes roles, or finishes a contract.
entries.memoryHook: Join -> provision. Leave or change roles -> de-provision.
entries.recognitionCue: Create appropriate access or remove access that is no longer authorized -> Provisioning/de-provisioning

entries.title: Permission Assignments and Implications
paragraphs: Permissions define actions such as read, write, execute, modify, delete, or administer. Every unnecessary permission increases the possible harm from mistakes, insider misuse, or a compromised account.
entries.recognitionCue: Grant the rights required for the role while considering what those rights enable -> Permission assignment

entries.title: Identity Proofing
paragraphs: Identity proofing verifies that an applicant really is the person they claim to be before the organization creates or trusts the digital identity. It commonly occurs during enrollment, credential issuance, or a high-value access request.
entries.memoryHook: Before issuing the identity, prove the real person behind it.
entries.recognitionCue: Validate a real-world identity before account trust -> Identity proofing

sections.title: Federation and Single Sign-On
paragraphs: Federation and single sign-on can work together, but they solve different IAM problems.

entries.title: Federation
paragraphs: Federation creates trust between separate identity domains. A service accepts identity information from an identity provider that already knows the user.
entries.recognitionCue: Trust an identity issued by another organization or domain -> Federation

entries.title: Single Sign-On (SSO)
paragraphs: Single sign-on lets a user authenticate once and reach multiple authorized services without entering credentials for each service again.
entries.recognitionCue: One authentication session reaches several authorized services -> SSO

table.caption: Federation and SSO
rows: Will one identity domain trust another?
Can one sign-in reach multiple resources?

sections.title: LDAP, OAuth, and SAML
paragraphs: The scenario's purpose usually reveals which identity technology is required: directory access, delegated permission, or a federated assertion.

entries.title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)
paragraphs: LDAP is a protocol for accessing and managing directory information such as users, groups, organizational data, and authentication-related records.
entries.recognitionCue: Query or manage directory information -> LDAP

entries.title: Open Authorization (OAuth)
paragraphs: OAuth provides delegated authorization. It lets one service receive limited permission to act on a user's behalf without receiving the user's password.
entries.memoryHook: You may access this resource on my behalf.
entries.recognitionCue: Delegated authorization without sharing the user's password -> OAuth

entries.title: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML)
paragraphs: SAML exchanges XML-based authentication and authorization assertions between an identity provider and a service provider. It is commonly used for enterprise federation and SSO.
entries.recognitionCue: Federated identity assertion used for enterprise SSO -> SAML

sections.title: Interoperability and Attestation
paragraphs: IAM systems must work together, and access must remain justified after it is granted.

entries.title: Interoperability
paragraphs: Interoperability allows identity technologies, applications, and platforms from different vendors or environments to communicate and function together.
entries.recognitionCue: Different IAM technologies exchange and use identity information successfully -> Interoperability

entries.title: Attestation
paragraphs: Attestation is a formal review or confirmation that an identity, entitlement, or access assignment is still accurate and appropriate.
entries.memoryHook: Does this user still need this access?
entries.recognitionCue: A manager or owner periodically confirms access remains justified -> Attestation

sections.title: Access-Control Foundations
paragraphs: Access controls determine who may use a resource and what actions are allowed. The model identifies how the decision is made.

entries.title: Access Controls
paragraphs: Access-control mechanisms enforce authorization policy for systems, data, applications, and physical or logical resources.
entries.recognitionCue: Determine who may use a resource and which actions are permitted -> Access controls

sections.title: Mandatory and Discretionary Access Control
paragraphs: Mandatory and discretionary models differ mainly in who controls the permissions.

entries.title: Mandatory Access Control
paragraphs: Mandatory access control (MAC) uses centrally enforced labels, classifications, and clearances. A resource owner cannot simply change the security policy.
entries.recognitionCue: Central labels and classifications enforce access -> MAC

entries.title: Discretionary Access Control
paragraphs: Discretionary access control (DAC) lets the resource owner decide who receives access.
entries.recognitionCue: The owner of the file or resource assigns permissions -> DAC

sections.title: Role-, Rule-, and Attribute-Based Access
paragraphs: These models can sound similar. Focus on whether the decision is driven by a job, a defined rule, or a combination of characteristics.

entries.title: Role-Based Access Control
paragraphs: Role-based access control (RBAC) grants permissions according to job function, such as Help Desk, Payroll, or Network Administrator.
entries.recognitionCue: A person's job determines permissions -> RBAC

entries.title: Rule-Based Access Control
paragraphs: Rule-based access control applies predefined rules or conditions, such as allowing access only during business hours.
entries.recognitionCue: A defined condition determines access -> Rule-based access control

entries.title: Attribute-Based Access Control
paragraphs: Attribute-based access control (ABAC) evaluates characteristics of the user, resource, device, and environment. A policy might require a Finance user on a managed device in an approved location.
entries.recognitionCue: A combination of user, resource, device, or environmental characteristics determines access -> ABAC

sections.title: Time Restrictions and Least Privilege
paragraphs: Authorization should be limited by both scope and, when appropriate, time.

entries.title: Time-of-Day Restrictions
paragraphs: Time-of-day restrictions permit access only during approved hours, even when the user otherwise has permission.
entries.recognitionCue: Access is permitted only during an approved schedule -> Time-of-day restriction

entries.title: Least Privilege
paragraphs: Least privilege grants only the minimum permissions required to perform the assigned task.
entries.memoryHook: Enough to do the job, and nothing extra.
entries.recognitionCue: Minimum necessary permissions -> Least privilege

sections.title: Multifactor Authentication Foundations
paragraphs: Multifactor authentication requires evidence from two or more different factor categories. Two credentials from the same category do not become MFA.

entries.title: Multifactor Authentication
paragraphs: MFA strengthens authentication by combining different kinds of evidence, such as a password and a security key. A password plus a PIN uses two knowledge items and is not true MFA.
entries.recognitionCue: Two or more different authentication factor categories -> MFA

entries.title: MFA Implementations
paragraphs: MFA can be implemented through biometrics, physical or software tokens, security keys, and other mechanisms that present evidence from different factor categories.
entries.recognitionCue: Mechanisms used to present multiple authentication factors -> MFA implementation

sections.title: Biometrics, Tokens, and Security Keys
paragraphs: The implementation tells you how the authentication evidence is produced or presented.

entries.title: Biometrics
paragraphs: Biometrics use measurable physical or behavioral traits such as a fingerprint, face, or iris.
entries.recognitionCue: A measurable human characteristic authenticates the user -> Biometrics

entries.title: Hard/Soft Authentication Tokens
paragraphs: A hard token is a separate physical authenticator. A soft token is software on a phone or computer that generates or provides authentication information.
entries.recognitionCue: Dedicated physical device -> Hard token; software authenticator -> Soft token

entries.title: Security Keys
paragraphs: A security key is a physical cryptographic authentication device that proves possession through interfaces such as USB or NFC.
entries.recognitionCue: Physical cryptographic authenticator -> Security key

sections.title: Authentication Factor Categories
paragraphs: MFA factors classify what kind of evidence proves the identity. The category—not the number of prompts—determines whether factors are different.

entries.title: MFA Factors
paragraphs: Security+ emphasizes knowledge, possession, inherence, and location as factor categories.
entries.recognitionCue: Categories of evidence used to verify identity -> MFA factors

entries.title: Something You Know
paragraphs: A password or PIN is knowledge held by the user.
entries.recognitionCue: Password or PIN -> Something you know

entries.title: Something You Have
paragraphs: A token, smartphone, smart card, or security key is a possession factor.
entries.recognitionCue: A possessed authenticator -> Something you have

entries.title: Something You Are
paragraphs: A fingerprint, facial characteristic, or iris pattern is an inherence factor.
entries.recognitionCue: A biometric characteristic -> Something you are

entries.title: Somewhere You Are
paragraphs: Location evidence can evaluate an approved office, expected country, or known network location.
entries.recognitionCue: Geographic or network location -> Somewhere you are

sections.title: Password Concepts and Best Practices
paragraphs: Password policy should make credentials harder to guess, limit the value of a stolen password, and help users maintain unique secrets.

entries.title: Password Concepts
paragraphs: Password concepts include the policy and technology decisions that govern password authentication.
entries.recognitionCue: Policies and technologies governing passwords -> Password concepts

entries.title: Password Best Practices
paragraphs: Good practice favors long, unique credentials, avoids reuse, protects stored secrets, and applies change requirements according to organizational risk.
entries.recognitionCue: Recommended controls for securely creating and managing passwords -> Password best practices

entries.title: Length
paragraphs: Length is the number of characters in a password. Longer passwords generally expand the guessing space.
entries.recognitionCue: Number of password characters -> Length

entries.title: Complexity
paragraphs: Complexity requires character variety such as uppercase, lowercase, numbers, or symbols.
entries.recognitionCue: Required variety of character types -> Complexity

entries.title: Reuse
paragraphs: Password reuse means using the same credential across accounts or password cycles. One compromise may then expose several systems.
entries.recognitionCue: The same password appears on multiple accounts or cycles -> Reuse

entries.title: Expiration
paragraphs: Expiration defines the point when a password must be replaced according to policy.
entries.recognitionCue: When a password must be changed -> Expiration

entries.title: Age
paragraphs: Password age tracks how long a credential has existed and supports minimum-age or maximum-age rules.
entries.recognitionCue: How long a password has been in use -> Password age

sections.title: Password Managers and Passwordless Authentication
paragraphs: Tools can reduce password reuse or remove the traditional password from authentication entirely.

entries.title: Password Managers
paragraphs: A password manager securely stores and manages credentials, helping users maintain long, unique passwords instead of reusing one memorable secret.
entries.recognitionCue: Secure vault for generating and storing unique account credentials -> Password manager

entries.title: Passwordless
paragraphs: Passwordless authentication avoids a traditional memorized password and may use a security key, biometric, or device-based cryptographic credential.
entries.recognitionCue: Authenticate without a reusable memorized password -> Passwordless

sections.title: Privileged Access Management
paragraphs: Privileged identities can make high-impact changes, so their permissions and credentials require stronger controls than ordinary user access.

entries.title: Privileged Access Management Tools
paragraphs: Privileged access management (PAM) tools control, monitor, and audit elevated accounts such as administrator, root, and service identities.
entries.recognitionCue: Secure and control elevated identities -> PAM

entries.title: Just-in-Time Permissions
paragraphs: Just-in-time (JIT) permissions grant elevated access only when needed and only for a limited approved period.
entries.recognitionCue: Temporary privilege is granted on demand -> JIT permissions

entries.title: Password Vaulting
paragraphs: Password vaulting stores privileged credentials in a protected central repository and can control retrieval, use, and rotation.
entries.recognitionCue: Privileged credentials are protected in a controlled repository -> Password vaulting

entries.title: Ephemeral Credentials
paragraphs: Ephemeral credentials are created for a short session or task and then expire, reducing how long a stolen credential remains useful.
entries.recognitionCue: Short-lived credential disappears after its task or session -> Ephemeral credential

table.caption: Privileged-access controls
rows: Limit when elevated permission is granted
Limit how long the credential exists

sections.title: Recognition Cues
paragraphs: Use the scenario's strongest clue to identify the IAM concept before comparing the answer choices.
bullets: Create or remove user access -> Provisioning / de-provisioning
Verify the real person during enrollment -> Identity proofing
Trust an identity across domains -> Federation
One sign-in reaches many services -> SSO
Directory access -> LDAP
Delegated permission -> OAuth
Federated identity assertion -> SAML
Review whether access is still needed -> Attestation
Central labels -> MAC; owner decides -> DAC
Job -> RBAC; condition -> rule-based; characteristics -> ABAC
Minimum permissions -> Least privilege
Different factor categories -> MFA
Physical token -> hard token; app token -> soft token
Protect elevated identities -> PAM
Temporary elevation -> JIT; protected repository -> vaulting; short-lived credential -> ephemeral

sections.title: Objective 4.6 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Authentication proves identity; authorization determines permissions. Identity proofing validates the real person during enrollment, while authentication verifies a returning user during access.

Federation establishes trust between identity domains; SSO lets one authentication reach multiple resources. LDAP accesses directories, OAuth delegates authorization, and SAML carries federated assertions.
MAC is centrally enforced; DAC lets the owner decide. RBAC follows job roles, rule-based access follows defined conditions, and ABAC evaluates attributes and context.
A password plus a PIN is still one factor category. A password plus a security key combines knowledge and possession and is MFA.
JIT controls when privilege is granted, vaulting protects privileged passwords, and ephemeral credentials limit how long the credential exists.
sections.callout: For IAM scenarios, ask: Who is the user? How do we prove it? What should they access? For how long?

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
paragraphs: Keep these final pairings ready for fast recognition.
bullets: Create account -> Provision; remove account -> De-provision
Prove real identity -> Identity proofing
Trust another identity provider -> Federation
One login, many services -> SSO
Directory -> LDAP; delegated permission -> OAuth; federated assertion -> SAML
Systems work together -> Interoperability; review access -> Attestation
System labels -> MAC; owner -> DAC; job -> RBAC; rule -> rule-based; characteristics -> ABAC
Approved hours -> Time-of-day; minimum access -> Least privilege
Password/PIN -> know; token/key -> have; fingerprint/face -> are; location -> somewhere
Physical token -> hard; software token -> soft; physical cryptographic authenticator -> security key
Unique credential storage -> Password manager; no traditional password -> Passwordless
Protect admin power -> PAM; temporary elevation -> JIT; lock admin credentials -> Vaulting; short-lived credential -> Ephemeral

miniCheck.intro: Choose the IAM technology that fits each part of the scenario.
miniCheck.prompt: A scheduling application asks a user to grant it limited access to the user's contacts without revealing the user's password. Separately, an employee opens a vendor portal after the corporate identity provider sends the portal a signed federated assertion confirming the employee's authentication.

fields.label: Technology for the scheduling application's limited delegated access
Technology carrying the corporate identity assertion to the vendor portal

miniCheck.correctFeedback: Correct. OAuth delegates limited authorization without sharing the user's password. SAML carries the federated authentication assertion from the identity provider to the service provider.
miniCheck.retryFeedback: Not quite. Look for delegated permission without password sharing in the first clue and a federated identity assertion in the second. Review LDAP, OAuth, and SAML, then try again.
